newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Soldiers vote on eve of Bosnia poll.
newsitem.headline: Soldiers vote on eve of Bosnia poll.

text.p: Selected polling stations opened in Bosnia on Friday to allow soldiers and police charged with maintaining security in Saturday's elections to vote early.
Around 3,000 military and civilian police and soldiers were expected to vote on the eve of the main election day.
Many thousands of police in Moslem-, Serb- and Croat-ruled sectors of Bosnia will secure the routes to be used by refugees to vote in still-hostile territory where they once lived.

NATO banned troop training or movements by factional armies during the elections as a security precaution. Local soldiers will not be involved in security on election day but were given the option of voting early.
Around three million people, around half of them war refugees, are eligible to vote in the internationally supervised elections, centrepiece of last November's U.S.-brokered Dayton peace treaty.

Voters will choose a collective presidency, parliament and regional assemblies that organisers hope will start the process of reuniting Serbs, Moslems and Croats now split into nationalist-ruled sectors carved out by conquest and expulsions.
The process has been widely criticised both in Bosnia and abroad for allegedly failing to meet Dayton's own terms for freedom of movement, association and expression.
Only a few soldiers and policemen had filtered into a dingy downtown ballot station in the Bosnian capital in the first few hours after it opened at 7 a.m. (0500 GMT).
The first voter at the central Sarajevo polling station was a 40-year-old Bosnian government army soldier who showed up with his wife pushing their baby daughter in a pram.

A security official scanned the soldier's hands with an infra-red device for invisible ink that would have indicated he had already voted. Finding none, the soldier was usherd into the shabby small room to a table heaped with ballot materials.

He held out his hands to be sprayed with invisible ink, then was given his ballot envelope which he took to an improvised booth -- an empty bookshelf partitioned into five sections by cardboard taped to the wall.
Election clerks had to wave away television cameramen who crowded behind the soldier to record the historic moment.
He strode over to a large cardboard box and dropped his ballot envelope through a slot, smiling bashfully for photographers.
Two Japanese election supervisors working for the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe OOSCE), which is in charge of the voting, were on hand in the station.

The OSCE is on the alert for election irregularities and fraud in a country brutalised by almost four years of vicious ethnic war. More than 2,000 supervisors and indepedent monitors were recruited to watch the vote.
"I hope things will get much better than before -- after four years of war it can hardly get any worse," the soldier, Salko Kobiljak, told reporters as he exited.

"I voted for the SDA. I have nothing to hide," he said, referring to the Moslem nationalist Party of Democratic Action led by Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic whose government controls only Sarajevo, central Bosnia and parts of the north.
"People should expect to work and not wear this uniform," he said, gesturing at his fatigues.

Another young Bosnian policeman in a green uniform, Suljo Curovac, 20, came in minutes later. He said he was a refugee from the Serb-held town of Rogatica in eastern Bosnia. "I feel good because I'm voting for the first time," he said.
